title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: We are not box pushers. We design the solution, we build the solution in India, and we support the solution for its entire life in the customer's data centre.
epigraph.author: Sanjay Lodha, Chairman & Managing Director, Netweb Q2 FY27 Earnings Call (26 October 2026)

web_blocks.html: Netweb sells six distinct product lines, but they share one commercial logic: the company engineers a complete computing system — compute, interconnect, storage, cooling, virtualisation and a software layer — rather than shipping a bare server. That integration is what lets a research institution, a bank or a sovereign cloud operator buy a working capability from Netweb instead of assembling one from components. The revenue mix has been transformed by AI over the last two years, and understanding each segment's role is essential to judging how durable the growth is.

web_blocks.takeaway: Two years ago AI Systems was a minority of revenue; by Q2 FY2027 it is 58.4%. The old backbone — HPC and private cloud — remains a genuine ~37% of revenue and is the part of the business least exposed to the AI-spending cycle.

web_blocks.html: AI Systems. This is now the engine. Netweb takes NVIDIA's reference architectures — most recently the Blackwell-based GB200/GB300 NVL systems — and adds its own chassis, liquid-cooling design, storage, networking and management software to deliver a validated cluster. Concrete example: in FY2026 Netweb won the order to build the AI infrastructure for India's foundational large language model, deploying a system powered by more than 5,000 GPUs. The customer is a sovereign AI programme that needed a nationally housed training cluster. The problem was that no off-the-shelf imported solution combined the scale, the confidential-computing requirements and the local-manufacturing mandate. Netweb engineered, assembled and integrated the cluster in India and supports it in place. Units are sold per node. For the ₹1,734 crore sovereign-AI order announced on 3 September 2025, each node carries an 8-GPU HGX-B200 configuration under the Tyrone Camarero platform, priced per node with a full-system service contract.

High-Performance Computing (Supercomputing/HPC). This is Netweb's oldest and most defensible line. Concrete example: the PARAM Yuva-II supercomputer deployed at C-DAC, Pune, in 2013. The customer is a national research and development agency. The problem is running large-scale scientific simulation — weather, materials, genomics — that a general enterprise server cannot handle. Netweb designed a hybrid architecture combining conventional processors with accelerators, built the cluster, installed the scheduling and middleware layer and tuned it for the specific workloads. It was paid on a project basis with an ongoing maintenance contract. More recently, in 2025 Netweb deployed a marquee supercomputing system for ISRO at its Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre. Winning these projects is a reference-based business. The customer will pay a premium for a proven domestic integrator, but will also cancel if a delivery slips.

Private Cloud & Hyperconverged Infrastructure. Concrete example: a regulated Indian bank that cannot place customer data on a public cloud. State Bank of India and IDFC First Bank appeared for the first time among Netweb's disclosed customers in FY2026. The problem is data sovereignty, security and regulatory compliance. The product is the Skylus private cloud and HCI stack, which bundles compute, storage, networking, virtualisation and automation into an on-premise estate the bank controls. Pricing is per rack or per node plus a software subscription and support, with a multi-year service element. This is the segment where recurring service revenue and switching costs are highest. Once a bank runs its core infrastructure on Skylus, ripping it out is expensive.

High-Performance Storage, Data Centre Servers and Software & Services. These are smaller but strategically important. The Tyrone ParallelStor VELOX storage platform uses parallel file systems and GPUDirect Storage to feed GPU clusters. A concrete example is a large-scale AI training job where the GPUs starve unless storage can stream data at hundreds of gigabytes per second. The storage is therefore sold as an integral part of the AI cluster rather than as a standalone box. The company's 2017 deployment of servers across 204 locations in 23 states for a public-sector surveillance project illustrates the Data Centre Servers line. There the challenge is distributed deployment and remote management rather than raw compute. And the Software & Services line — KUBYTS container images, Skylus.ai orchestration, FMOcean data pipelines — is the glue that lets Netweb claim 'full-stack' rather than 'component supplier'.

web_blocks.title: Is the AI Segment a Moat or a Mix Shift?
paragraphs: Notice a subtlety in the mix. AI Systems jumped from a minority to nearly 60% of revenue in six quarters, but that jump came disproportionately from a handful of very large deals — two strategic orders worth roughly ₹2,184 crore announced in FY2026, plus the sovereign LLM cluster. Meanwhile HPC and private cloud, the slower, stickier businesses, have kept growing but now look small beside the AI line.

This matters because it splits the company's durability question in two. The HPC and private-cloud segments have decade-long customer relationships, 75.6% repeat revenue and genuine switching costs — that is where a defensible business lives. The AI segment has explosive demand and world-class technology partners, but it is also where competition is fiercest (global OEMs and Taiwanese ODMs sell comparable boxes), where the customer decides on price and delivery speed, and where a single quarter's revenue can swing on the timing of one order. The mix that looks most impressive on the income statement is not necessarily the mix that is most protected.

web_blocks.html: Management's own framing reinforces the concentration question. On the Q2 FY2027 call, an analyst asked how fast Netweb grows outside its top five customers. The CFO pointed to 449 new customers added in the first half alone. He stressed that the top-five and top-ten lists are not static cohorts but rotating groups of 25 to 30 accounts. That is a reasonable mitigation, but it is not the same as diversification. 75.6% of FY2026 revenue still came from repeat customers, which is a double-edged statistic. It proves retention but also implies a concentrated base. The honest reading is that Netweb has a diversified customer list but a concentrated revenue base, and the two should not be confused.

book_paragraphs: Come with me into what Netweb actually sells, because the headline 'AI company' label hides six different businesses stitched together under one roof. The cleanest way to see them is through the customer's problem. A national laboratory wants to simulate a jet engine; a bank wants its customers' data to stay inside its own walls; a sovereign programme wants to train a language model on GPUs it physically owns; an enterprise just wants servers that work. Netweb's insight, built up over twenty-five years, is that all four of those buyers will pay a premium for a single vendor who engineers the whole machine rather than shipping a box.

Start with the segment that now dominates the income statement: AI Systems. Picture the order Netweb won in FY2026 to build the infrastructure for India's foundational large language model — a cluster powered by more than 5,000 GPUs. The customer is a national AI programme; the problem is that training a frontier-scale model needs thousands of accelerators wired together with the right interconnect, cooling and storage, and no imported turnkey solution existed that simultaneously met the scale, the confidentiality and the made-in-India mandate. Netweb took NVIDIA's Blackwell reference architecture, designed its own chassis and liquid-cooling, integrated storage and orchestrator software, assembled and validated the cluster in Faridabad, and now supports it in place. That is a ₹-thousands-of-crores project sold node by node, and it is why the AI line exploded from 43% of FY2026 revenue to 58% of revenue by Q2 FY2027.

Now step back to the business that actually built this company: high-performance computing. In 2013 Netweb deployed PARAM Yuva-II at C-DAC in Pune, and in 2025 it delivered a marquee supercomputer for ISRO. Ask yourself what those customers were really buying. They were not buying a faster processor; they were buying a guarantee that a complex scientific workload would run, on time, on hardware they could support, from a vendor they could call at 2 a.m. Netweb's edge here is reference and trust, accumulated over 600 supercomputing installations and seventeen appearances in the global Top 500 list. This is slow, defensible, premium business — and it is the part of Netweb least dependent on the AI frenzy.

The third pillar is private cloud. Here the concrete example is a large Indian bank. SBI and IDFC First Bank surfaced as Netweb customers in FY2026, and the reason is regulation: a bank cannot simply move customer data to a hyperscaler and hope for the best. Netweb's Skylus platform lets the bank stand up its own cloud — compute, storage, networking, virtualisation and automation, all on-premise — and once the bank's core systems run on it, switching away is genuinely painful. This is where recurring service revenue and lock-in live, which is why the segment's 24% of FY2026 revenue punches above its weight in strategic value.

Do not overlook the smaller lines, because they are the connective tissue. The Tyrone ParallelStor VELOX storage platform exists because a GPU cluster is useless if it starves for data — so storage is sold as part of the AI system, not beside it. The surveillance project that put Netweb servers in 204 locations across 23 states in 2017 shows the company can do distributed deployment, not just big iron. And the software layer — KUBYTS containers, Skylus.ai orchestration, FMOcean data pipelines — is what lets management credibly call the company full-stack rather than a component reseller.

So watch the mix, and notice how it splits the durability question in two. On one side sit HPC and private cloud: slower growth, longer relationships, 75.6% repeat revenue, real switching costs. On the other side sits AI Systems: explosive growth, elite technology partners, but also the shark tank where Dell, HPE, Lenovo and the Taiwanese ODMs compete on price and delivery, and where one order's timing can swing a quarter. The mix that makes the income statement thrilling is not the mix that makes it safe.

One more honesty test before we move on. On the Q2 FY2027 call, an analyst asked how fast Netweb grows outside its top five customers. The CFO's answer was that the company added 449 new customers in the first half and that the top-five and top-ten lists are not fixed — a rotating pool of 25 to 30 accounts shuffles through those positions every few years. That is a fair point, and it is also a reminder that a long customer list is not the same as a diversified revenue base. When you underwrite Netweb, hold both facts at once: it is winning new logos fast, and it still depends heavily on a small number of very large accounts.

Let me leave you with the question that governs this whole segment story. When a sovereign programme or a bank chooses Netweb over Dell or HPE, what exactly is it buying? It is not buying the fastest chip; everyone has access to the same NVIDIA silicon. It is buying a vendor who will design to its specific workload, manufacture the machine inside the country, integrate storage and software, and stand behind it for years. That is a real service, and it is worth a premium, as the 75.6% repeat-revenue figure shows. But ask yourself how wide the gap really is between Netweb and a global OEM that decides to localise. The premium lives in the integration and the eligibility, not in anything a competitor cannot eventually copy. So the segment mix you have just walked through is best read as a portfolio of good businesses with one fast, crowded one on top.

book_callouts.title: The Integration Premium — and Its Limits
book_callouts.text: Every segment on this page is really a variation of one promise: buy the whole system from us and it will work. That promise is worth real money when the customer is a research lab, a bank or a sovereign programme with a complex workload and no appetite to integrate it themselves. It is worth much less when the customer is a cloud operator who can buy a near-identical box from a global OEM or an ODM and simply wants the lowest price per GPU. The same integration capability that earns a premium in HPC and private cloud is worth far less in the AI-systems shark tank.
